annotation.name: service_calls_low_day_charge
annotation.hypothesis: Customer-service calls raise the predicted churn risk steeply once a customer has made several of them while daytime use is low or average; for heavy daytime users the calls make little difference until the count is high. Self-probe (the typical customer, with daytime minutes and day charge set together): at 120 daytime minutes ($20.40 day charge) the predicted risk is 1% with 0 calls, 16% with 3 and 70% with 4; at 180 minutes ($30.60) it is 3% with 2 calls, 13% with 4 and 57% with 5; at 240 minutes ($40.80) it is 15% with 0 calls, still 15% with 6 and 38% with 7. So the number of calls at which risk takes off moves up as the day charge rises. In the training data, the 156 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge under $30 churned at 75.6% (mean predicted risk 65.5%), and through this part their score is on average 5.30 above the part's training average; the 162 customers with 4 or more calls and a day charge of $30 or more churned at 25.3%, and for them the part adds 0.20 on average. Switching the part off lowers the training AUC from 0.901 to 0.759. Mechanism: two hinged units (node 104 and node 7506) open as calls rise and close as the day charge rises; each feeds the score directly and through a follower unit (7664 and 9029). Small extras: New Hampshire and Connecticut indicators enter node 104, and a Florida-specific unit (node 2039) opens on 3 training rows, so it is fitted to those rows. The formula evidence rounds coefficients to three significant figures (off by up to 0.016 on the part's output over the training rows).
